analysis.one_liner: Imposes binding pollution limits and deadlines to restore the Chesapeake Bay.
analysis.headline: The Senate environment committee approved the bill in September 2010, but it died at the end of the 111th Congress without ever coming to a Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the Clean Water Act's Chesapeake Bay Program to require the six Bay states and DC to adopt enforceable watershed plans cutting nitrogen, phosphorus, and sediment pollution, with a Bay-wide pollution limit (a TMDL) set by EPA and full implementation due by 2025. It paired those mandates with federal grants — including roughly $1.5 billion authorized for stormwater projects and dedicated technical-assistance money for farmers — plus an interstate nutrient trading program and a ban on phosphorus in cleaning agents. States that missed deadlines could lose funding and face federal takeover of their plans. The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee reported the bill favorably in September 2010, but it never received a vote in the full Senate before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, fish, and recreate around the Chesapeake Bay — the bill's stated purpose was to cut nitrogen, phosphorus, and sediment pollution so state water quality standards can finally be met. It also directed guaranteed shares of grant money to farm and forest technical assistance and to the smaller headwater states.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each Chesapeake Bay state to adopt a watershed implementation plan with enforceable pollution limits for nitrogen, phosphorus, and sediment, fully implemented by 2025.

Directs EPA to establish a Chesapeake Bay-wide total maximum daily load (a pollution budget) and an interstate nutrient trading program, and gives the agency backstop authority — including withholding funds and writing its own plan — if a state falls short.

Makes missed state commitments subject to enforcement, including lawsuits by citizens, and requires annual public action plans and progress reports so the public can track whether cleanup is actually happening.
Authorizes roughly $1.5 billion for stormwater pollution control grants to local governments, plus implementation grants, stewardship grants, and nutria eradication funding.
Sets new controls on polluted runoff from development and bans phosphorus in most cleaning agents, targeting the fastest-growing source of Bay pollution.

analysis.who_pays: The direct costs would fall on pollution sources: farms facing nutrient limits, developers required to manage stormwater runoff, wastewater treatment plants subject to tighter permits, and state and local governments funding compliance — costs typically passed on through utility bills and taxes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Farms, developers, utilities, and state budgets

drawbacks.text: Cleanup is expensive, and the costs fall on real people: upgrades to sewage plants, stormwater systems, and farm practices are typically financed through utility bills, local budgets, and food prices.

The bill leans on a new interstate nutrient-credit trading market, an approach whose benefits depend on credits reflecting real pollution reductions — a mechanism critics have long warned can be gamed or shift pollution locally.

Agriculture is named in the bill's own findings as one of the largest single-sector sources of the pollution, so the plan inevitably imposes new obligations on working farms, even with the compliance shield and technical-assistance set-asides.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside — enforceable deadlines and backstops for restoring the nation's largest estuary, which supports fisheries, recreation, and local economies across six states — was large, and the bill paid for a meaningful share of it with grants rather than unfunded mandates. The costs were real but narrow: farms, developers, wastewater utilities, and ultimately state budgets and ratepayers would bear cleanup expenses, and some of the money would flow through a new nutrient-credit market whose effectiveness depends on careful EPA oversight. The bill also explicitly shielded fully compliant farmers from new federal enforcement, softening the burden. On balance a well-designed, if expensive, restoration program.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate environment committee reported the bill favorably in September 2010 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but no senator ever brought it to the floor for a vote, and the Congress ended in January 2011 with the bill still waiting.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Senator Cardin on October 20, 2009, with Senators Mikulski, Carper, and Kaufman, and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.
The committee held a subcommittee hearing on November 9, 2009, and on June 30, 2010 ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.

On September 28, 2010, the committee reported the bill with written report No. 111-333 and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 620) — the waiting line for floor time.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never came to a vote in the Senate or the House, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Polluting sources — farms, developers, and dischargers — avoided new enforceable pollution limits and the compliance costs that would have come with them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farms and developers spared new limits

against.what_they_did: Never brought the reported bill to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Agricultural and development interests opposing Bay regulation
against.what_they_did: Farming and building-industry groups actively opposed the bill's enforceable pollution limits for agriculture and new development during the 2010 debate.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and no Senate floor vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record shows whether broader support existed across parties.

industries.industry: Agriculture (farms and agribusiness in the Bay watershed)
industries.note: Agriculture is identified in the bill as one of the largest sources of Bay pollution, so states would have imposed new enforceable nutrient limits on farm runoff. The bill cushions this with guaranteed technical-assistance funding and exempts fully compliant farms from new federal enforcement.
New large developments would have to restore pre-development stormwater flow or pay compensation, raising the cost of building on hardened surfaces.

Permits would carry nutrient limits consistent with the Bay-wide TMDL, driving costly upgrades paid through ratepayers, though a nutrient trading program would let plants buy cheaper reductions elsewhere.
The bill requires states to ban phosphorus in most cleaning agents within three years, with narrow EPA hardship exemptions.

industries.industry: Chesapeake fishing, seafood, and recreation industries
industries.note: A restored Bay supports commercially and recreationally important fisheries and public access, which the bill's findings describe as a multibillion-dollar regional economic force.
